NSF Grant Proposal Pathways To Cybersecurity Careers Submitted April 2022 The U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics predicts the growth in cybersecurity employment demand will be 34% in the near future.
This is projected to cause over 700,000 unfilled cybersecurity jobs in the U.S., costing the U.S. economy billions of dollars.
While there exists this dramatic shortage in the cybersecurity workforce, there is a parallel phenomenon that only 4% of entry level cybersecurity positions currently go to people classified as from low-income backgrounds.
This Track 2 S-STEM project, called Pathways To A Cybersecurity Career (P2CC), will support low-income students to graduate with a Master’s degree in Cybersecurity from the University of Rhode Island (URI), and enter the cybersecurity workforce.
The P2CC project will provide yearly scholarships of 1-3 year durations to at least 42 unique recipients over 6 years, with expected retention and graduation rates being at least 90%.
The scholars will be domestic low-income students with academic ability, talent/potential, and with demonstrated unmet financial need.

They will be recruited by a campaign that targets traditionally under-represented groups in the cybersecurity field including women, rational/ethnic minorities, and differently-abled people.
Selection of scholars will be by a panel that has been trained in potential selection biases when evaluating low-income applicants, using a rubric that is designed for equity.
In addition to providing scholarships, the P2CC project will implement curricular and co-curricular interventions for the scholars that will target cognitive and non-cognitive aspects of low-income students’ experiences and success that focus on academic supports, and on increasing the students’ professional identity through exposure to the cybersecurity workforce and professional skills, professional role modeling, participation in student cohorts, faculty mentoring, and building self efficacy.
Intellectual Merit.
The interventions of the P2CC project will adapt, implement, and study the application to cybersecurity education of evidence-based curricular and co-curricular interventions that have been shown to be effective supporting low-income student recruitment, retention, and success in STEM education.

The P2CC project’s primary intervention uses Fitzgerald’s definition of “professional identity” as: “containing the attributes: skills and functions; knowledge values and ethics; personal identity; group identity in the profession; and the influence of the context of the field”.
It applies to cybersecurity education specific professional identity enhancement techniques that Peters has classified as “high impact” for low-income STEM student success, and that have been demonstrated on similar S-STEM projects in Math, Science, and Computer Science.
The project includes a robust evaluation of its primary objectives: 1) produce at least 42 graduates who enter the cybersecurity workforce, 2) evaluate the effectiveness of the support interventions in supporting the success of low-income cybersecurity students, and 3) disseminate the results to assist degree programs at other institutions in supporting the success of low-income students in their cybersecurity education.
The evaluation uses data sources including pre and post surveys of scholars, exit tickets following specific activities, exit interviews, demographic data, academic assessments, and career placement data.

The evaluation performs formative evaluation of the objectives using a formal Plan-Do-Study-Act continuous improvement process, and summative evaluation to facilitate reporting and academic publication.

Broader Impacts. This project impacts the scholars themselves, all of which will be low-income students, by providing them access to a high-quality graduate education in cybersecurity - something that is unattainable by many due to economic hardship, and the lack of available financial aid at the graduate level. The professional identity and academic enhancement interventions will help ensure the success of these scholars. The broader impact will be on both the U.S. cybersecurity workforce, which lacks numbers and diversity of workers , and on the U.S. economy as a whole. By producing more qualified cybersecurity workers from low-income background, the P2CC project will serve as an initial step in starting to tap a woefully untapped talent pool that will help address a U.S. cybersecurity workforce deficit crisis that is costing billions of dollars in losses to the nation’s economy, and affecting international competitiveness of U.S. companies.

The need to attract more underrepresented groups (URG), including women and racial/ethnic minorities, into the cybersecurity field is well-documented [48,49,50,51].
The goal of this SFS program is at least 40% women and at least 1 of each 5-student cohort being from other URGs.
The URI CS Department has a Broadening Participation in Computing (BPC) Committee and several initiatives in place, and the CS Department Chair and others are attending the 2020 NSF-sponsored CRA workshop series on establishing BPC plans for CS departments [XX].
The PI will have an Individual NSF CISE-format BPC plan, and the CS Department will have a BPC plan, in place in 2020 (see attached letter of commitment).
Included in these efforts, the URI CS Department recently hired a staff member dedicated to BPC initiatives.
This CS BPC Coordinator will work with the PIs and partner organizations at URI (see attached letters of collaboration) to implement an aggressive recruiting plan to recruit SFS candidates from URGs.

Aspects of this recruitment plan include: ● Recruitment material.
We will work with URI chapters of the National Society for Black Engineers and Women in Computer Science (see letters of collaboration) to ensure that our SFS program recruiting material (web sites, flyers, messages in classes and events) is effective for a diverse audience of students.
The National Center for Women in Technology’s [52] (NCWIT) Recruit Strategically resources [53] will be employed.
These include techniques to deliver effective messaging strategies to target audiences such as URI women undergraduates and regional high school students.
NCWITs template strategic recruitment plans [54] and Roadshow In a Box [55] will be adapted to SFS candidate recruitment using their techniques for effective messaging to women [53]. ● Recruitment opportunities.
There are populations of URG students on which we will focus recruitment.
Some of them are: ○ The Community College of Rhode Island.
As described above, CCRI has high populations of racial minorities and first-generation college students in its cyber program.

We will present the SFS opportunity in CCRI cybersecurity classes, train advisors on it, provide flyers, post posters, and have an SFS information session on CCRI’s campus each year (see attached letter of collaboration). ○ URI Talent Development (TD) [56] .
This program recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come to URI from historically disadvantaged backgrounds, a majority of whom are students of color.
They come to campus the summer before their Freshman year to participate in a college-preparation program that includes taking college courses.
PI Fay-Wolfe coordinates a CS course in the TD program every summer with 40 TD students.
The course has a module on cybersecurity during which the SFS opportunity will be showcased. ○ URI Chapter of the National Society For Black Engineers (NSBE-URI).
NSBE-URI runs several programs to motivate and encourage youth of color to pursue an interest in CS and engineering majors.
These include events such as development workshops, where students and corporate representatives share their experiences in areas such as resume writing and interviewing techniques.
NSBE-URI also has academic and corporate representatives speak to its undergraduates about research and work opportunities.

NSBE-URI has committed to including cybersecurity, and the SFS program in particular, in its workshops for the duration of this SFS project (see attached letter of collaboration). ○ URI Women in Computer Science. URI’s Society For Women in Computing (SWiC) is an undergraduate organization where women in the CS Department regularly meet to explore Computer Science. The URI SWiC group has committed to helping us recruit undergraduate women for the SFS opportunity including hosting an SFS information session at one of their meetings each year of the project (see attached letter of collaboration). The SFS scholarship selection process will be conducted such that when we have a pool of qualified candidates, addressing increased participation by URG students will be a primary consideration in making SFS scholarship offers within that pool.

Manhattan Institute is now issuing templates for dismantling DEI educational initiatives in every state across the country WHEREAS Florida is at the forefront of a nationwide campaign to silence Black voices and erase the full and accurate history and contemporary experiences of Black people WHEREAS Florida College System presidents issued a collective statement affirming their view that some diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives are harmful to higher education WHEREAS Governor DeSantis has explicitly stated his aim to defund and dismantle DEI initiatives as well as the governing body and administrative leadership of The New College, a public institution WHEREAS Governor DeSantis and the Florida House of Representatives made demands in January for information regarding the funding of programs related to diversity, equity, inclusion, and critical race theory at colleges and universities, now intending to bar funding for these programs across the higher education system WHEREAS under Florida's Stop WOKE Act— which has been temporarily enjoined by a federal court from being enforced in higher education settings— endorsement of theories that criticize systemic racism is forbidden, disparagement of these theories is openly allowed and transgressions can be penalized through revoking millions of dollars in state funding WHEREAS public universities and colleges in Florida must nevertheless administer ideological surveys to all higher ed students, faculty and staff, the results of which may be used to drive budgetary decisions WHEREAS students in Florida are nevertheless permitted to seek permission for recording lectures, which may be used in disciplinary or legal actions against faculty WHEREAS all syllabi and reading lists must nevertheless be posted in publicly accessible locations at least 45 days before the start of classes WHEREAS faculty speech in Florida is nevertheless unconstitutionally compelled in some quarters to expose students to ideas they may find “uncomfortable, unwelcome, disagreeable, or offensive,” through syllabi, reading selection and class discussion WHEREAS Governor DeSantis rejected the AP course in African American History, demanding that The College Board excise specific subject areas from the curriculum WHEREAS The College Board stripped down and altered the AP exam for African American History, followed by a statement of regret for failing to immediately denounce the Florida Department of Education and Governor DeSantis's administration, the latter of which commented that African American Studies “lacks educational value.” WHEREAS Governor DeSantis is considering barring all Advanced Placement Exams in Florida

WHEREAS investigations target trans students and employees by demanding information that could potentially compromise patient privacy and discourage individuals from seeking medically appropriate care WHEREAS Black leaders, alarmed by Governor DeSantis, have begun to protest and prepare for 2024 WHEREAS higher education workers are organizing around the country, through growing unions like the United Faculty of Florida (UFF) and new coalitions like Higher Education Labor United, to defend our freedoms and throw a much-needed lifeline to the sinking discussions about higher education in Florida and elsewhere WHEREAS the United Faculty of Florida are welcoming statements of support for their fellow colleagues and associated communities in Florida WHEREAS it is vital that students, faculty, staff, and administrators outside of Florida band together in this moment of crisis to defend the public good of higher education ____________________________________________________________________________________________________________ THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Faculty Senate of URI extends this statement of solidarity and support to our fellow colleagues and associated communities in Florida.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this statement confirms URI's current statement of Foundational Values in espousing a commitment to freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good, as well as an inclusive, accessible, equitable and diverse community whereby we respect the rights and dignity of all.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that in issuing this statement of support, the University of Rhode Island aspires to serve as a national model for the role a flagship public research university can play in driving transformative change for the betterment of its state and the global human condition.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this statement applauds the URI Board of Trustees' affirmation of the university's determination to embrace Rhode Island ’s heritage of independent thought, valuing creativity and scholarship, diversity, fairness, and respect, engaged learning and civic involvement, and intellectual and ethical leadership.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this statement affirms our commitment to the ideals of the URI Office of Community, Equity and Diversity and its core values of advancing equity, inclusion, and diversity in the global community and modeling honesty, integrity, and social justice.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this statement explicitly stands by the URI Cornerstones, acknowledging the University of Rhode Island as a principled community guided by values, including the principles of independent choice, intellectual curiosity, open-mindedness, free expression, the rights and dignity of each individual and group, working to understand and respect differences, and the rejection of prejudice, discrimination, and intolerance.
